about: CLI-agnostic catalog of what counts as a credential value worth substituting before it reaches a model, a brief, a command, session history or memory. Detection is by CONTEXT (a value next to a sensitive key name, an auth header, a URL password, a known token shape) or by the explicit <private> fallback -- never by "looks random": a bare hash or a UUID is never flagged on its own, because commits and checksums are pasted constantly and must survive untouched. Every regex is anchored so it only fires on the shape it names; every consumer (an adapter plugin, a test) reads this file rather than retyping the patterns.
whitespace_note: The ONE definition of whitespace, the body of a character class, for every engine: JavaScript, Python and Go disagree about `\s` (Python matches U+001C to U+001F and U+0085 but not U+FEFF; JavaScript the reverse; RE2 only ASCII), so no pattern uses `\s` for it. The patterns below carry these characters literally, and so do the consumers that build a pattern in code. The members are written as JSON escapes: the parser turns them into literal characters, so no engine needs a regex-level `\u`.
never_detected: a bare 40-hex string (a git commit hash)

key_context.keys_note: A key is matched by its WORDS, not its spelling: the text captured from a message is split on `_`, `-` and camelCase boundaries (a lowercase letter or digit followed by an uppercase one, or an uppercase one followed by an uppercase and a lowercase one), so `dbPassword`, `DB_PASSWORD` and `db-password` are all [db, password]. It names a sensitive key when its WORDS equal a catalog key's words or END with them (`JWT_SECRET_KEY` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` end with `secret_key` and `secret_access_key`; `clientSecret` ends with `secret`). `secret_key` and `secret_access_key` are listed as keys of their own because `key`/`access_key` alone are not sensitive words.
key_context.quoted_value_note: One unit of a quoted value: any character that is not the quote or a backslash, or a backslash and the character it escapes. A quoted value is `quote + body{min,} + quote`, so an escaped quote (`\"`) never closes the value early and leaves its tail in clear. The two alternatives start with different characters, so there is nothing to backtrack into.

skip_unquoted_if.name: function_call
skip_unquoted_if.note: a value shaped like `getToken()` is a call, not a credential -- pasted code must survive.

skip_unquoted_if.name: call_open
skip_unquoted_if.note: `os.environ.get(`, `strings.Trim(` -- an unquoted value stops at the first quote or space, so a method call with arguments reaches the scan cut right after its open parenthesis, and `function_call` (which wants the closing one) cannot see it. Only a value that ENDS at the `(` is skipped: `Passw0rd(2024`, `abc(12345678` and `correct.horse(battery` go on after the parenthesis and are still detected.

skip_unquoted_if.name: dotted_call_empty
skip_unquoted_if.note: `lexer.get_token()`, `os.getcwd()` -- a dotted name called with no arguments. At least one dot and empty parentheses: it is a method call, and nothing a person types as a password.

skip_unquoted_if.name: shell_or_template_var
skip_unquoted_if.note: `$VAR`, `${VAR}`, `%(name)s` -- an interpolation placeholder, not a literal value.

skip_unquoted_if.name: sensitive_word_value
skip_unquoted_if.note: `this.password = password`, `token: accessToken` once lowercased -- a value that is just the name of a sensitive thing, in lowercase, is a reference to a variable. It is a whole-value match, so `mysecretpassword` is still detected.

skip_unquoted_if.name: bare_identifier_no_digit
skip_unquoted_if.note: a value made only of letters reads as another variable name, a type or a word, not a literal secret, when it is short (1 to 9 letters), a Capitalized word (`Whitespace`, `Signature`: a class or type name), all capitals, has an underscore or `$` in it (snake_case, CONSTANT_NAME), or has a lowercase letter followed by a capital (camelCase). A lowercase word of 10 letters or more (`DB_PASSWORD=secretpass`, `password: correcthorse`) IS detected: a password without digits is still a password. The 10-letter floor is measured, not guessed: at 8 letters a scan of the Python standard library flagged assignments like `token = nextchar` and `pwd = expected`, which are code. Accepted false negatives: a password of 9 letters or fewer with no digit, one that is Capitalized, camelCase or all capitals, or one with an underscore; quotes or `<private>` catch them. A value with a digit is never identifier-shaped under this pattern and is always detected.

sensitive_suffix_header.note: Any header whose NAME ends in one of these suffixes, whatever it is called -- X-Aco-Joven-Signature, X-Auth-Token, X-Client-Key, X-Hub-Signature -- or in one of them followed by exactly one -<digits> segment (`allow_trailing_digit_segment`), the real shape of GitHub's own webhook-signature header, X-Hub-Signature-256 (and, generalized, X-Signature-512). The variable name derives from the header name itself, not a fixed rule name. X-Signature-Version and X-Api-Key-Version do not match: they end in -Version, not in -Signature/-Key or -Signature/-Key plus digits.

url_credentials.name: url_password
url_credentials.note: The leading lookbehind anchors where a match may START: without it, a long run of scheme-class characters with no `://` anywhere (no scheme at all) makes the engine retry the same expensive backtrack at every position in the run -- O(n^2) on a large paste. Anchoring means that backtrack happens at most once per run, not once per character in it.

known_formats.name: private_key_block
known_formats.note: The lazy `[\s\S]+?` rescans to the end of the text from every BEGIN that has no END after it, which is quadratic on a paste of many BEGIN lines. A match ends at an END line, so the pattern runs only on the text up to the end of the line holding the LAST occurrence of `requires_literal`, and not at all when there is none. The matches are the same ones.

known_formats.name: private_key_unterminated
known_formats.note: a key block whose END line never arrived (a truncated paste, a cut log line): the BEGIN line, then any RFC 1421/OpenPGP armor header lines, one optional blank line, and the base64 lines of 16 characters or more that follow, up to the first line that is none of those (the newline before that line stays). At least one key line is required: a lone BEGIN line holds nothing to hide. It runs after `private_key_block`, so a complete block never reaches it. The last line of a key is often shorter than 16 characters and stays visible; it holds no usable part of the key.

nesting.note: Before the two patterns below run, every span is rewritten as one flat span in canonical lowercase (a close tag closes the innermost open one; overlapping or nested spans merge): a nested open/close pair inside it is dropped, an open tag with no close takes the rest of its line (the rest of its paragraph when nothing else follows the tag on the line) and is closed there, a tag between backticks is a mention and not a tag, and a close tag with nothing open is left alone. The patterns themselves stay flat. The same rewrite runs before the `<private>...</private>` -> `[REDACTED]` fallback.

named.note: captures NAME and value; NAME is used verbatim (normalized)
